newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - S.African economy needs African peace.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - S.African economy needs African peace.

text.p: South Africa is pursuing a twin-track foreign policy to bring stability to the continent it shares with some of the world's poorest countries and to forge supportive economic alliances with partners elsewhere, says Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad.

"Unless we tackle the issue of conflict prevention and peacemaking on the African continent, we can't really deal with our other strategic approach to the continent -- the economic one," he said in an interview.

"Clearly, without economic development and exploitation of our potential, we will continue to decline. There would be no hope of escaping Africa's status as the only area of the world where living standards are still declining."
Pahad, energetic deputy to seldom-seen Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo, sees economic growth and political stability as mutually reinforcing goals for the country and the continent.
South Africa's commitment to peace and stability in Africa was demonstrated, he said, by:
-- President Nelson Mandela's so far inconclusive bid to broker a truce in Zaire;
-- South Africa's commitment of 2,000 troops to a specialist peace-keeping unit that could in future be seconded to an African peace force;
-- its efforts to promote the Southern African Development Community (SADC) as the primary arena for regional cooperation in trade, politics and peace-making.
AFRICAN RENAISSANCE IS REAL
"We have always believed that with a strong SADC, we would be able to play a greater role on the African continent to achieve what everyone now refers to as the African Renaissance.

""We're trying to use all our efforts -- not in isolation, but through the SADC, the OAU (Organisation of African Unity) and increasingly through the U.N. and the European Union -- to coordinate efforts to stabilise the continent," he said.

Without an end to the civil and ethnic wars tearing at the heart of the continent, South Africa would be damned with the rest of Africa and could be swamped by refugees looking for a haven from conflict.

"Generally, investors perceived Africa as a dying continent and sought other areas for investment. Now I think there is a more positive perception being accepted ... the bigger powers are seeing Africa as a new area of potential.
"We've been through the political phase of Africa's rise and now its time for the economic phase. The renaissance is real," he said.

South Africa's own economic success would be central to the economic revival of the continent and Mandela's government was seeking strategic alliances with countries outside Africa that could help the country and the region, Pahad said.
"Our objective is a stable South Africa and we have come to the conclusion that our political stability has to be underpinned by economic development.
"Unless we start dealing with the expectations of the people, we could start running into some serious instability problems. We have to create the conditions for economic growth."

South Africa has crafted a macroeconomic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR, which is designed to boost annual growth from a disappointing 3.1 percent in 1996 to six percent by the turn of the century.

But Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said in his March 12 budget he was forced to downgrade the growth forecast for fiscal 1997/98 to 2.5 percent, which is not enough to slow the growth of unemployment.
SEARCH FOR ECONOMIC ALLIES

Pahad said the departments of foreign affairs and trade and industry were cooperating to identify potential economic allies outside of Africa and business was being drawn more and more into the search.
He said China, currently 15th amongst South Africa's trading partners, was accepted as the major focus of new trade and investment, but he added:

"We have targeted strategic countries where we think we need to put more emphasis. Mexico, Chile and Argentina are, for example, countries with which we can develop much more aggressive relations," he said.
Pahad said other countries with which South Africa would seek a special relationship included India, Malaysia, Singapore, Saudi Arabia and Brazil.

"This does not mean that our traditional partners are not important -- the European Union remains our major trading partner -- but we might be reaching towards ceilings in our trade and investment with some of these countries and we've got to identify oher opportunities."
He said South Africa would seek bilateral deals to promote trade and investment within the rules of the various trade and political blocs to which countries might belong.
"We all agree on the need to move away from command economies and on the need for multi-party democracy ... but many of us believe that development must be sustainable and affect the lives of people.
"We have to bridge the gap between richer and the poorer countries," Pahad said.
